name: J Dilla
hook: A Detroit producer who switched off his sampler's timing correction and taught musicians a new way to feel rhythm.
blurb: James Yancey grew up in Detroit, and Pete Rock was his hero. As Jay Dee and later J Dilla, he produced for Slum Village, A Tribe Called Quest, The Pharcyde, Common and Erykah Badu. What he changed was rhythm. Working on the Akai MPC3000 mostly with the timing-correction setting, quantise, turned off, he layered parts with different, deliberately uneven timing. His drums do not land exactly on the beat: some hits come a bit early, some a bit late, so the rhythm seems to lean. Dan Charnas's biography calls it Dilla Time, and it crossed back from programmed music into live playing, as drummers started learning to play like his machine. He was a Detroit figure in the full sense: his 2001 album Welcome 2 Detroit rewrote Kraftwerk's 'Trans-Europe Express' hook as a tribute to the way his city took in European electronic music. He was ill for years with a rare blood disease and lupus, and died in February 2006, aged 32, three days after his album Donuts came out. Donuts is often said to have been made mostly in hospital, but Charnas's biography disputes it. It began as a shorter beat tape made at home in Pro Tools, most of it before his hospital stays, and Stones Throw's art director Jeff Jank expanded it into the released record after Dilla suggested the label do that itself. He did keep working on it in hospital. His MPC3000 and Minimoog Voyager are now in the Smithsonian.
